content: Mauveine, also referred to as aniline purple or Perkin's mauve, holds the distinction of being the first synthetic organic dye. Its chemical name is 3-amino-2, ±9-dimethyl-5-phenyl-7-(p-tolylamino) phenazinium acetate. The molecular formula for mauveine A is C26H23N4+ X−, while mauveine B is represented as C27H25N4+ X−. Mauveine was discovered accidentally in 1856 by an 18-year-old chemist, William Henry Perkin. At the time, Perkin was attempting to synthesize quinine, an anti-malarial drug, as part of a challenge posed by his professor, August Wilhelm von Hofmann. During one of his experiments, Perkin oxidized aniline using potassium dichromate. Under these conditions, the aniline reacted with toluidine impurities present in the mixture, resulting in the formation of a black solid. Such outcomes were common in unsuccessful organic syntheses. However, while cleaning his flask, Perkin noticed that a component of the black solid dissolved in alcohol, producing a purple-colored solution. This solution turned out to be an effective dye for silk and other textiles. Perkin patented this new dye and, in the following year, established a dye manufacturing facility in Greenford, London, along the Grand Union Canal, to produce it on a large scale. Initially, the dye was marketed under the names aniline purple or Tyrian purple, the latter being a reference to an ancient natural dye derived from mollusks. By early 1859, the dye was named mauve in England, derived from the French word malva, which refers to the mallow flower. Chemists later referred to it as mauveine. Mauve gained immense popularity in 1862 when Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom appeared at the Royal Exhibition wearing a mauve silk gown. However, by the late 1860s, mauve fell out of fashion as newer synthetic colors emerged. Despite this, mauveine had already secured Perkin's fortune and marked the beginning of the synthetic chemical industry. In the early 20th century, the National Association of Confectioners included mauveine among the approved food colorings, under various names such as rosolan, violet paste, chrome violet, anilin violet, anilin purple, Perkin's violet, indisin, phenamin, purpurin, tyralin, Tyrian purple, and lydin. Subsequent research on chemical dyes also contributed to the accidental development of modern chemotherapy, as seen with sulfonamides. The distinctive color of mauveine became widely recognized due to its use in spirit duplicator printing machines (commonly known by the trade name Ditto), which were popular in the mid-20th century. Modern laboratory synthesis of mauveine involves dissolving a mixture of aniline, p-toluidine, and o-toluidine in sulfuric acid and water in a roughly 1:1:2 ratio, followed by the addition of potassium dichromate. The molecular structure of mauveine proved challenging to determine and was not definitively identified until 1994. Mauveine is, in fact, a mixture of four related aromatic compounds that differ only in the number and placement of methyl groups. Mauveine A is composed of two molecules of aniline, one of p-toluidine, and one of o-toluidine. Mauveine B, on the other hand, incorporates one molecule each of aniline, p-toluidine, and o-toluidine. In 1879, Perkin demonstrated that mauveine B is related to the safranines through the oxidative or reductive loss of the p-tolyl group. Safranine itself is a 2,8-dimethyl phenazinium salt, while the parasafranine produced by Perkin is presumed to be the 1,8or 2,9-dimethyl isomer. In 2007, two additional components of mauveine were isolated and identified. These were named mauveine C, which features an additional p-methyl group on mauveine A, and mauveine B2, an isomer of mauveine B with the methyl group located on a different aryl group.
